prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, whose magic-wavelength trapping brought optical timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: After the full first round I move my preferred configuration from B057 to B027. The deciding factor is not that the topological case has weakened as science, but that the committee has shown me, and I have to agree, that the credit for B057 cannot be stated cleanly. The Kane and Mele proposal and Molenkamp's HgTe measurement are real milestones, but the HgTe quantum-well prediction that the experiment actually tested was made by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and Zhang's death means that gap cannot be repaired. Six of eight members have also placed the lattice clock first, and none disputes the experimental claim. The physics of B027 is verified in the way I trust most: Katori's magic-wavelength scheme removes the light shift that would spoil a trapped-atom clock, Ye's strontium clocks took it to about 1e-18, and independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN, PTB, NIST, SYRTE) reproduce the performance. The theory of the atomic structure that fixes the magic wavelength can be computed and has been compared with measurement, which is the link between calculation and spectra that I value. The credit is a clean pair. Since the clock has already shown something about nature, in redshift tests across millimetres and in many-body physics inside the lattice, I think the citation can state a physical result and not only a technical figure.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection to B027 is novelty. The 2005 prize honoured the frequency comb and laser-based precision spectroscopy, and the 2012 prize honoured control of single quantum systems including ion clocks. Ye's career sits close to the first of these, and a third award in the same neighbourhood of metrology could be criticised. The discovery content is also a capability rather than a surprise from nature, and the fundamental results so far are tighter bounds rather than a new effect. The Sr-lattice contributions of Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and Oates are outside the two-name credit, and the SI second has not yet been redefined, so timing can be argued either way. Against my own earlier preference I should also say that B057 would have been the better prize in terms of conceptual novelty, a new class of quantum matter, if the credit were clean. I give up that point only because the attribution cannot be made clean with three names.

responses.point: Mehlig, also a supporter of B057, asked whether the citation could be framed around the Z2 concept and the observation without implying that the HgTe prediction is unrecognised, and argued that the 2016 prize covers topological invariants in model systems whereas Kane-Mele and Molenkamp classify real band insulators.
responses.response: I agree with your answer on the 2016 overlap and I would still make it. On your credit question I have tried to write the citation and I do not think it can be done without either leaving out the HgTe prediction or implying that the Kane-Mele proposal and the Molenkamp measurement were a single step. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang supplied the quantitative band-inversion calculation, which is exactly the kind of first-principles prediction I weigh most heavily, and a citation that silently omits it would misstate the record. With Zhang deceased and the three-person limit, I no longer think B057 should lead, and I would hold it as the first alternative for a later year if the committee can reach a more defensible three-name framing. I would ask you whether you can accept B027 this year on those terms, since you called it a fully legitimate winner in your own round-1 statement.

responses.point: Danielsson argued that the credit for B057 is not clean because Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and the 3D contributors are missing, that Zhang's death makes the omission unrepairable, and that the committee must settle what B057 adds to the 2016 prize first. He also wants the B027 citation to rest on what the precision has shown, namely redshift tests and many-body clock physics, so that it does not read as a third award for better clocks.
responses.response: You are right on the credit, and this is the main reason I have moved. I also take your wording point on B027 and I have tried to meet it. My citation names magic-wavelength trapping, which is the new element in the lattice clock and is not part of either the 2005 or the 2012 citations, and the 1e-18 level as the result. I am wary of putting redshift tests into the citation text itself, since those results are tight bounds and not a discovery, but I would support the committee's explanatory note stating that the clock has already tested gravity and measured many-body effects in the lattice. On novelty relative to 2005 and 2012, my judgment is that the comb provided the ruler and the ion work showed how to control a single quantum system, while confining millions of neutral atoms with the light shift cancelled is a different idea with different physics. I would not describe it as a mere application.

responses.point: Olsson asks whether Ye is the originator or the developer of Katori's concept, whether the early lattice-clock groups (Takamoto, Lemonde, Ludlow) disturb the two-name credit, and notes that B057 has too many open attribution questions to lead.
responses.response: On B057 I now agree with you. On B027 I think the Katori and Ye credit can be defended but the wording should be honest about the roles. Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice, and Takamoto in his group made the first demonstration, which is the part I cannot place in a two-name credit. Ye, with his group, then demonstrated clocks at the 1e-18 level with the full systematic evaluation, and the cavity-stabilised laser and cryogenic work that made this possible. A citation that says 'invention and development' covers both without claiming that Ye originated the scheme. I think the committee should accept that a two-person limit leaves out Takamoto, Lemonde and others, as the Prize always does, but I would like the explanatory note to say so openly. Whether the redefinition of the second has to come first is, for me, a timing question and not a scientific one, since the performance is already established by several independent clocks.

responses.point: Kroll asked whether to wait for the redefinition of the second, and said he would defer to Mehlig and me on whether the three-name B057 credit is robust.
responses.response: I thank you for the deference, and I should answer it directly. I do not think the three-name credit for B057 is robust, so you should not defer to me on it. On waiting, my answer is that the science has matured independently of the redefinition. Several clocks at the 1e-18 level are compared over fibre and via satellite links, and the redefinition is a decision of a metrology body that follows the science. Waiting would lose little, as I said in round 1, but acting now also costs little, and a prize for the lattice clock that comes just before the redefinition does not make the Prize dependent on a standards decision. I would not support waiting only for that reason.

uncertainties: Whether Ye's role is original invention or decisive development of Katori's concept, and whether the citation wording 'invention and development' is enough. I am working from memory on the early priority record, including the role of Takamoto and colleagues.

Whether the committee will read the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes. I believe it is, because of the magic-wavelength trapping, but this is the point on which B027 could fail.

Whether B057 could be given a defensible three-name credit by a different configuration (for example one built around Kane, Mele and Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang priority), which I cannot judge without the nomination record, and which the death of Zhang makes impossible to repair completely.
Whether the redefinition of the second should come first, which I treat as a timing question and not as a scientific one.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. I have no known personal or institutional tie to Katori, Ye, Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Bloch, Greiner or Zoller. As a theorist of electronic structure and magnetism I am professionally close to topological-materials and Hubbard-model physics, which I treated in round 1 as a possible bias toward B057 and B006 and not as a recusal matter. I changed my preference away from B057, so that bias does not now work in favour of my configuration. I am far from atomic and precision-measurement physics and I rely on Lindroth and Kroll for the technical details of the clock.
